utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is case number IT-04-82-PT, the Prosecutor versus Ljube Boskoski and Johan Tarculovski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm Dan Saxon, together with my colleagues Ms. Joanne Motoike, Ms. Meritxell Regue, Mr. Matthias Neuner, and our case manager, Ms. Lakshima Walpita.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Appearing for Mr. Ljube Boskoski, Edina Residovic, attorney-at-law; Guenal Mettraux, co-counsel; and Jesenka Residovic, case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Apostolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. For Mr. Johan Tarculovski, Antonio Apostolski; Jasmina Zivkovic, co-attorney; Marija Sandeva, case assistant; and Jordan Apostolski, case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'll just inquire now whether each accused are able to receive the proceedings in a language they are understanding. First Mr. Boskoski. THE ACCUSED BOSKOSKI: [Interpretation] We are able to hear, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. You are hearing as well, Mr. Tarculovski? THE ACCUSED TARCULOVSKI: [Interpretation] I hear it as well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, of course the purpose of this hearing is the -- what's programmed to be the final pre-trial conference before we commence the hearing on Monday of next week; that is, the hearing of the trial of this case. This Trial Chamber, as you are aware, has now been finally and formally assigned to conduct the trial. As counsel should by now be aware, we must finish this conference in the course of this morning. So counsel are encouraged to be extremely succinct in any submissions that they make. Could I mention that the Chamber is aware of and has before it a number of, on the most part, very recent motions that have yet to be the subject of formal decision. For the Prosecution, we have four motions. Two filed on last Tuesday. There's been no opportunity yet for either Defence to respond to those. One which was filed a little earlier, and one accused has responded on Tuesday of this week and not the other. The fourth is to do with the last of the seven 92 bis/92 ter motions, which is ready for delivery, but we understand that one Defence team has something further that they wish to advance about it. So we are poised waiting to see what that might be before the decision is delivered. For the two Defence teams, there are altogether now nine motions; five of them for the Boskoski Defence, which are ex parte. They were all filed in the course of this last month. The decisions in them will all be delivered in the course of next week. There is a motion by the Boskoski Defence for leave to file late submissions. There is one challenge to the Prosecution expert evidence, and there is an indication again from the Boskoski Defence that they propose or wish to seek leave to file something further in respect of that. There is then a further Boskoski Defence motion to stop the Prosecution's process of investigation and disclosure. It was filed last week. The Prosecution replied on Tuesday. The Chamber has given some preliminary consideration to it but is not in a position to publish its final written decision. We would indicate at this stage that the motion will not succeed. The formal decision will be delivered in writing in the course of next week. There remains a joint motion to delay the start of the Prosecution evidence, which was filed within the last week. The Prosecution's reply was received late yesterday. We will, no doubt, discuss further the implications of that motion in the course of this hearing. Now, that was a quick summary of the motions that the Chamber has. It will be apparent from what we have said that there really is - to borrow the language of one of the submissions before us - a flurry of last-minute activity by, in particular, two of the three teams. Some of that is a little disquieting. It suggests that Prosecution -- that preparation is not as advanced as it ought to be for at least two of the teams. That leaves Mr. Apostolski sitting rather serene there, but perhaps it is that he's just got his trial counsel. We may hear more of him in the very near -- his assisting counsel. We may hear a lot more from him in the near future. I'm not encouraging you, Mr. Apostolski. Having dealt with those motions in that brief way, I think it's best to stay with them and try and put them aside. Mr. Saxon, is there any one of your motions about -- that are outstanding about which you wish to put anything very briefly to us that isn't included in the written submissions we have?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Saxon. Now, Ms. Residovic, is there anything concerning any of your outstanding motions about which you want to put any further brief submissions to the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my colleague, co-counsel, will just briefly inform you of our indication that we are about to submit a motion related to Prosecution's expert witnesses. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Your Honours. Simply to give you or to confirm the indication which we gave yesterday in our response to the Prosecution application to amend the statement or the report of Mr. Bezruchenko. As we indicated in our filing, we will file in the coming days further submissions as regards the admission of the reports of both Mr. Bezruchenko and Mr. Burgess, two of the Prosecution proposed experts. We will seek to do so as early as possible and hopefully by the middle of next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You realise that, I believe, at least one of them is listed in the first group of Prosecution witnesses. Am I right there, Mr. Saxon?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Respectfully, I believe you are not right, Your Honour. We are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Splendid. Okay. I was foreseeing a problem that doesn't exist. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: That would be all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You were just telling us about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. We wanted to give an indication to the Prosecution as well so they could make any preparation that would be necessary. We will try to file that at the earliest possible time and hopefully by the middle of next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You realise, A, you will need to seek leave to do that because you're well out of time for doing it; and, B, we have decisions ready. So you're asking us to take on board something entirely new and reconsider our decision; is that what you'll be doing?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, we'll do our best to make it simpler rather than more complicated for Your Honour, but, yes, we will seek leave to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And may we ask, are you challenging the conclusions or the qualifications?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, at this stage --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Or what is the -- about the expert?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, at this stage, the challenge will essentially be to the expert's nature of the proposed evidence as well as to the requirements of independence on the part of the proposed expert, at least one of them. So for the time being, the challenge will be essentially on those two points.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So no other of the submission -- the motions of the Boskoski Defence require any further submissions at this point?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Apostolski, is there any matter that you wish to put about any of the outstanding motions?

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have nothing to add with regards to outstanding motions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, in summary from all of that, as long as we receive the proposed additional Defence material by the middle of next week, which is Wednesday, we will consider whether or not leave should be granted to receive that further material; and in light of that decision, deal with the motion dealing with the expert witnesses. Otherwise, the Chamber will proceed now to finalise and publish its decisions in respect of all of the other outstanding motions. Now, that, Mr. Saxon, brings us logically to a review of how you see your case, firstly, with respect to number of witnesses; and secondly, the number of exhibits; and thirdly, the time-frame.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, as you know, the Prosecution recently submitted a motion which requested partly leave to remove three witnesses from its witness list. That motion is now pending.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Of course, the Chamber also very recently provide -- granted leave to the Prosecution to add two witnesses to its list. As counsel for the Defence will attest, mathematics is not my -- my strong point. I don't want to give you a quick figure right now as to the number of witnesses. What I had done last night was actually calculate time. I had calculated hours in terms of the expected length of the Prosecution's case. If you would indulge me, I'd like to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You would like us to be content with time, would you?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Perhaps for the moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Because what I did is I looked at the recent decisions of the Trial Chamber regarding the Prosecution's motions related to the admission of written evidence pursuant to 92 bis and 92 ter. And as you know, of course, the Trial Chamber partially granted some of those motions, but what that meant is an additional amount of time will be necessary to present the Prosecution's case. In June of last year, when the Prosecution submitted its last motion or revised 92 bis motion, the Prosecution submitted to the Chamber that the Prosecution's case would take approximately seven court weeks if all of these motions were granted. Now, with the decisions that were issued last week, there will be 43, 92 bis or 92 ter witnesses who must come for cross-examination, and that will add approximately 64 and a half hours to the Prosecution's case. Plus, there are four witnesses for which the Prosecution had sought permission to submit their evidence in writing, but for whom the Chamber would like to hear viva voce. And in the Prosecution's estimation, that will add an additional 12 hours to the Prosecution's case, for a total of 76 and one-half additional hours. However, when I factored in the witnesses for whom we believe will be removed from the list, with the leave of the Chamber, and the two witnesses for whom the Chamber has recently granted leave to add to our list, it's my calculation that the length of the Prosecution's case will increase now by an additional 75 hours, which, if you use 3.75 hours as a measure of a court day, that works out to 20 court days additional, which would be an additional four more weeks of court time. And that means, Your Honour, that by my calculations, rough as they may be, the Prosecution's case in chief would last for approximately 11 weeks in total.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, thank you for that, Mr. Saxon. Can we inquire a little about your estimate of time for cross-examination. Now, has that been done? Because that's a notoriously difficult exercise, and the result is often wildly unreliable.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: In the Prosecution's calculations, Your Honour, we included the estimated time for cross-examination as well. For example, with an additional viva voce witness for whom I estimated three hours of testimony, that was an hour and a half of direct examination and an hour and a half of cross-examination. That was our estimate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So you've equalled time for examination and cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That's how we did our calculation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, that's how the Prosecution did its calculations, yes, Your Honour. May I say, Your Honour, as you noted earlier, there is still one motion outstanding related to the use of written evidence, and of course that could alter these calculations a bit depending on the decision of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So you've not made any calculations based on some guess as to the outcome of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Mr. Saxon. Could I turn now, Mr. Saxon, to that old subject of disclosure, just to inquire whether Rule 66 remains completed and translations complete and to inquire where we are with Rule 68.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect to Rule 68, as you know, searches are ongoing and we are continuing on an updated basis to review material and to disclose any material that we find -- that we deem to fall within Rule 68. With regard to Rule 66(B), Your Honour, we continue to review our collections, the items in our possession. And just last night, I want you to know that we disclosed some additional material under Rule 66(B). With respect to Rule 66(A)(ii), we are up-to-date, Your Honour. A number of translations have come in recently and have been disclosed to the Defence. It's my understanding that every translation that we have received to date we have disclosed. We are still waiting for some translations from CLSS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can you say how many of those are outstanding?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I hesitate to give you an exact figure. I'm told it is -- it is not a lot of material, but -- pardon me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we come back to that later, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour, all exhibits that require -- are required to be translated into the language of the accused, all proposed exhibits, have been translated and disclosed. The only thing we are waiting on now are some English translations of items that were not originally in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. And you'll give us an estimate of the number of that in the course of this morning. Now, Mr. Saxon, there were a number of matters which you indicated you would like to raise in the course of this morning. Would you like to deal with each of those in turn?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, one matter the Prosecution would like to raise is the question of when the parties should alert the other party to the materials they intend to use, either in direct examination or in cross-examination. I had sent a letter previously to counsel for the Defence, suggesting that for this trial we initiate a procedure whereby the Prosecution, during the Prosecution phase, would alert the Defence at least two days before the start of direct examination, of which exhibits it intended to use during the direct examination of that particular witness. And I suggested also that the Defence also agree to alert the Prosecution at least two days in advance of which materials it intends to use during the cross-examination of the same witness. And if such materials are not in the possession of the Defence, if they could be provided. We haven't -- the Prosecution has not received a response to its letter. Since then I've done a bit of research. I know, for example, in the Mrksic trial, I believe there was a rule whereby the parties had a one-day deadline, a 24-hour deadline, before the start of witness testimony to exchange this information. I know that in other Trial Chambers, it's a much tighter deadline. This information is exchanged actually at the start of -- well, materials to be used during cross-examination, that information is provided to the Prosecution right at the start of direct examination or at the close of direct examination. The Prosecution recommends a slightly larger window of perhaps of at least one day for the exchange of this information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The experience of the Chamber in its trials led us to try in the Mrksic trial with one day, and that didn't work as well as it should have in practice because there was a lot of last-minute difficulty always over documents. So from the point of view of the smooth running of the trial, 48 hours, that is two days, is much more practical.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The Prosecution would certainly be in accord with that suggestion, Your Honour; in fact, that was the Prosecution's original suggestion to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That is where we were with earlier trials. I'll hear other submissions on that matter, Mr. Saxon. Ms. Residovic or Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my colleague, Mr. Mettraux, will respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Yes, good morning, Your Honour. We would like to make further submission in relation to this issue. We've also reviewed the procedure before the Tribunal, the practice of various Trial Chambers, and indeed Mr. Saxon has relied upon Your Honour's ruling in the Mrksic case, where you have ordered the parties to disclose the material to be used in cross-examination 24 in advance of the beginning of the evidence. The Mrksic decision seems to be quite a solitary decision in that regard, if I may say so. In the Milutinovic, Popovic, and Dragomir Milosevic case, the Trial Chambers have ordered that the material be disclosed to the Prosecution at the commencement of the examination-in-chief. In the Babic, Matic, and Prlic case, they've asked the Defence to disclose that material before the start of the cross-examination. In the Halilovic case, the Trial Chamber repeatedly refused to impose any obligation regarding disclosure of cross-examination material upon the Defence. The reason for the Trial Chamber to do so, if I may, was that the Rules themselves do not provide for any obligation upon the Defence in that regard. More fundamentally, however, is the principle of effectiveness of the right to confrontation. The Defence is very concerned that if it has to disclose material which may, for instance, go to the credit of a witness, the effectiveness of the right to confrontation may be undermined. There may also be a situation where the rights against self-incrimination may be at stake, if, for instance, the Defence has not been able to make a final determination as to whether it intends to use material in cross-examination or not, and often enough this determination may only be made after the end of the examination-in-chief. The concern of the Defence is also one which relates to the nature of the system before this Tribunal. In a civil law system, Your Honour, the investigation would be led by an investigative judge and not by a party. Furthermore, the practice before this Tribunal of proofing does not exist in most civil law system or any -- that I know in any case. Our concern is that material which could be critical to the establishment of truth and the ascertainment of truth with a witness could and would probably be put to the witness during a proofing session, which may contribute to perhaps a lesser degree of truth being revealed during the cross-examination. The practice, as mentioned above, has seemed to go back to an obligation on the part of the parties to disclose that material prior to the -- shortly after the commencement of the examination-in-chief. For example, in the Milutinovic and Prlic case, the Trial Chambers had granted orders of the sort which Your Honour has granted in the Mrksic case, and later on in the trial have come back upon this practice to impose a new rule whereby the Defence should disclose that material shortly after the commencement of the examination-in-chief. The Defence believe that this practice would better protect the fundamental rights of the accused. We would be happy to obviously comply with that practice if that's acceptable to Your Honour. But as I mentioned earlier, one type of material which is of particular sensitivity in that regard would be any sort of material which would go to the credit of the witness. Obviously, if a witness such as an expert is coming, there may be good reason why the parties could agree to give earlier notice to the other side if we intend to use a large amount of material or regulations. I think this is a matter that can be dealt with directly between the parties to find an agreeable solution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could I mention, Mr. Mettraux, that one of the problems of what you are proposing, looking at it from the point of view of the Rules, which are essentially adversarial and not inquisitorial, that is not civil system, you are getting down to an absolute trial by ambush, if you understand that terminology. The consequence of that when you cross-examine on something that is not known to the Prosecution or the witness or not foreseen, is that there usually needs to be an adjournment before re-examination to enable that matter to be investigated and looked at, and the result then is, A, a lengthening of the trial; B, the loss of momentum of hearing the evidence of the witness because the witness has to be held for a day or two, or a week or two while a matter is investigated. And the consequence of all of that adversely affects the flow of the trial. You mentioned that these are matters that are of confidence, but of course you realise that under Rule 65 ter (F) there are obligations about disclosure on the Defence which occur pre-trial, which are generally not observed and which we are not insisting on observance. So that the disclosure of documents a little before may involve a momentary revealing to the Prosecution at the last moment of some matters, but do not go as extensively as the Rules might contemplate over some other matters. The further observation I would make is that this practice was followed in the Mrksic trial, three accused, very experienced Defence counsel, and never once was it suggested that it interfered in their presentation of their case or had an effect adversely to the rights of their clients. We were watching that carefully. We were thinking even of moving it to 48 hours, but the problem that you foresee, the fundamental intrusion into the rights, was not experienced by the very experienced Defence counsel and their clients in that case. I think part of your concern may stem from your familiarity with a civil law system trial, which is so very different, about the information that is known to the Bench and available to the parties from that in an adversarial trial. Now, I mention those matters in case there's something further you would like to put about any of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, very, very shortly, Your Honour. I think the issue of intrusion is one that would not apply to each and every witness. As I mentioned earlier, there would be witnesses, that's the experts, in relation to which there should be no issue of concern in that regard. We believe, however, that there are a number of witnesses which are going to be presented by the Prosecution in relation to which the Defence would be very concerned to have to disclose the material in advance of the person giving his evidence, in particular if the witness is proofed after the Defence has disclosed that material to the Defence [sic]. In relation to ambush, Your Honour, I understand the expression. The Defence may say that this is certainly not the intention of the Defence of Mr. Boskoski to ambush the Prosecution, and as we mentioned earlier we will seek to cooperate and collaborate with the Prosecution in relation to those matters as much as we can. The experience that I've had from the Halilovic case is there has been absolutely no delay in relation to any of the witnesses in relation to this matter, and to the extent that we can cooperate again with the Prosecution in that regard, we would be happy to do this. Many of the documents which the Defence would seek to use are also Prosecution exhibits. To that extent, there should be no issue in relation to those documents. As I mentioned earlier, I think that the issue is really related to a small group of Prosecution-proposed witnesses. To the extent that the Chamber would be willing to grant some sort of flexibility to the Defence, for instance, by seeking leave in relation to particular witnesses or to trust that the parties will seek to collaborate in that matter, and if problems arise in the course of the trial at this stage perhaps it would be more appropriate for the Trial Chamber to give that sort of order. But at this stage, it is our submission that it's a bit early to impose that obligation upon the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Apostolski, is there any submission you would like to make in addition to what we have heard?

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I completely support the presentation of my colleague, Your Honour, and I thereby think that in respect to the direct hearings, that the 24-hour deadline is sufficient for submission of the written documents, while for the cross-examination I think that the written documents could be submitted immediately before the cross-examination. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: In the view of the Chamber, the position should be that the -- during the Prosecution case, the Defence will give to the court registry officer 48 hours' notice of all documents they want taken out of their private electronic file so that they are available when called on the electronic system. Now, that is not disclosure to the Prosecution or to the other Defence party; it's merely enabling the registry to ensure that the documents are ready and can be brought up on the electronic screen as needed by the parties. For expert Prosecution witnesses, the Defence should give 48 hours' notice to the Prosecution of the documents each Defence intends to use during cross-examination of that expert. For other witnesses, the normal position will be that the Defence should give 24 hours' notice to the Prosecution of the document it intends to use. But there will be a proviso that the Defence may within that 24-hour time, that is no later than 24 hours, give notice in writing to the Prosecution and to the registry and to the Chamber's court officer that it is withholding documents going to the credit of that witness. We will proceed on the basis experimentally that that is not abused. If that concession is abused, we will review the position, but where a Defence has a document it feels is material and which it feels could be -- its effect could be compromised by a disclosure 24 hours before, as long as notice is given that documents are being withheld, the Chamber will allow that to occur, and those documents should then be disclosed as the evidence-in-chief of the witness commences. I think by this measure we will try to meet the difficulties concerning Mr. Mettraux and Mr. Apostolski, whilst at the same time trying to ensure a reasonably smooth flow of the case. It's, as I emphasise, experimental. If it's being overused, we will have to reconsider the concession. And if it is the case that the Prosecution is significantly embarrassed by lack of notice about a document, we may have to consider some adjournment of the re-examination of that witness. But otherwise, we think those orders may meet the various practical and professional needs of the various parties and of the Court. Could I also mention -- is there something, Mr. Saxon, you want to raise about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. I didn't hear in your directive a requirement for the Prosecution, a temporal requirement for the Prosecution, to provide notice to the Defence of exhibits it will use in its direct examination. And I just wanted to alert you to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm just turning to that, Mr. Saxon. You're anticipating me. Thank you. Now, during each week of evidence, that is if the Chamber isn't sitting during a week this can be ignored, but when evidence is being given during a week, as will normally be the case, the Prosecution is to notify the Defence teams and the Chamber and the court officer of the witnesses it intends to call during the following two weeks. So always we are two weeks ahead. And in that notice for each witness should be an estimate of the time that the Prosecution anticipates for examination and cross-examination, so that the Chamber can maintain a watch over the timely progress of the evidence of each witness. The Prosecution should then 48 hours before a witness is called give notice to each Defence team and the court registry officer of the documents it intends to use during the evidence of each of its witnesses. We would only add that each team of counsel should be aware of the need to provide the documents it intends to use during the case to the registry in electronic form well before the witness is to be called, so that they can be included in the electronic court system in an orderly and proper way. Now, when they're brought into the system, they're first of all included in the confidential private file of the party, so they're not disclosed to others, but they are then loaded into the system in good time. The advance notice of the documents which we've mentioned, 48 hours for some, 24 hours for others, and at the time of commencement of the evidence for a few, is the time when each party authorises the release of that document from the confidential private file so that it then becomes available to the other parties. I hope you all understand that. Now, cooperation by all parties in this is very important for the smooth flow of the trial. The Chamber is well aware that genuine unexpected situations do arise. I'll call them emergencies. When it has not been foreseen that a document will be used, something occurs during the evidence of the witness and a document is then thought to be necessary. The Chamber will watch to ensure that there are genuine emergency situations. If they do occur, either during examination or cross-examination, the court registry officer can't include that document in the electronic system. So what has to happen is the party will need to have a -- hard copies of the document for use for that witness. You may find if the emergency is noticed 24 hours before and it's not in the electronic system, the court officer may be able to include it; but if not, it will be necessary for hard copies of those documents to be available. They'll be needed, one for each of the three Judges; the court registry officer; the court Chamber's officer; the witness; other parties; and interpreters. Given that we have five languages, all told they'll need, I think, to be 14 copies of any document that isn't in the electronic system. Some documents, such as large detailed maps and charts, are not suitable for use in the e-court system. There is simply too much information on them for them to be able to be viewed reasonably. With such documents, you'll need to have hard copies available so that they can be used during the trial. There are some documents which counsel will anticipate to be very important and which you may want also to have a hard copy available so -- in particular, so that the Judges may make notes on those documents and deal with them in a more hands-on user way than is possible even with the electronic noting system of the e-court. And we have found in a number of trials that counsel quickly get a feel for the sort of document they would like the Judges to have in hard copy, as well as electronic form. We would also mention that as we are using more than one language, the document can only be displayed on the screen in one language, and you may well find that you will need for important documents to have hard copies in English for the Chamber and perhaps for the other parties, if the document, for example, is being displayed in Macedonian so that the two accused can follow it. So please keep those matters in mind as you prepare during the case. Now, what we have indicated applies during the Prosecution case for the times. The same will apply, but in reverse, during the case of each accused, so that we will appreciate that all parties will be dealt with on an equal basis in this matter. So the time-limits presently placed on the Defence for their cross-examination will, when the Prosecution has finished its case and the Defence case is proceeding, those times will apply to the Prosecution for their cross-examination and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, I hope that's given sufficient guidance about practical matters in the handling of exhibits and documents and notice to the other party to enable the trial to get underway smoothly. Now, Mr. Saxon, there were further matters?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]. Thank you. Briefly, one statistic that you asked for a few moments ago. At this time, given recent decisions about adding and removing witnesses from the Prosecution's witness list, the Prosecution expects to receive the evidence of 96 witnesses in total, in different form, written, viva voce, and expert, et cetera. The total number is 96.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's your anticipated number of witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour. Your Honour, briefly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I can only say you're ambitious with 11 weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The Prosecution is optimistic, Your Honour. We will do the best we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You'll find the Chamber can be even more optimistic and a fairly determined task-master --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If time is not being used efficiently, the Chamber will be fairly quick to get counsel to move on to something that matters rather than spending time on side matters. Just be on notice of that. Clearly, everyone will be aware that it is in the interests of everybody, especially the two accused, for the trial to be completed as quickly as possible, consistently with giving all parties a fair opportunity to present their case. We don't want to just waste time unnecessarily. So we'll be watching that throughout the hearing. Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, an additional matter that the Prosecution wanted to raise this morning deals with the amalgamated, or if I may use the term consolidated 92 ter witness statement that the Trial Chamber has asked the Prosecution to prepare for those witnesses who will be testifying before the Chamber under Rule 92 ter and for whom there is -- there is more than one prior ICTY statement. The Chamber directed the Prosecution that for such witnesses, in order to increase clarity and efficiency and avoid confusion, the Prosecution should create a consolidated statement of the prior statements for the purposes of submitting that consolidated statement under Rule 92 ter. And the Prosecution is -- has already commenced that effort, indeed I believe there are two witnesses scheduled to testify next week who fall into this category. The Prosecution, with leave of the Chamber, pursuant to any comments Defence counsel may make, intends to do the following: We will create these consolidated statements. Obviously, the prior statements have already been translated and disclosed in a language that the accused understands, so that material has been available to the Defence for quite some time now. But after we create a consolidated statement and a witness arrives here in The Hague, we will then read that consolidated statement - in most cases using an Albanian-speaking interpreter - we will read that consolidated statement to the witness prior to the witness coming into the courtroom, to give the witness an opportunity to say, There's a mistake there or I have something to add, something is wrong that needs to be corrected. We would then record any such information and attempt to immediately translate that new information, be it an addendum, some additional information, a correction, and attempt to translate it into the language of the accused before the witness begins to testify so that the rights of the Defence under Rule 66(A)(ii) are also respected. That is what the Prosecution proposes to do, and we wanted to alert the Trial Chamber and the Defence of what the Prosecution proposes and plans to do to see if there are any comments or concerns.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, there seem to be two matters that are distinct which you have put together as one. The first is the consolidation. The -- many of the statements where there were two and, at times, even three from the one witness which you sought to have admitted pursuant to 92 bis, as those statements were looked at quite -- sections of them were simply repetitive and the Chamber sought a consolidation that removed any repetition. So there would be one single statement. As we now have the advantage of Rule 92 ter, that new statement didn't require the formalities of signature and witnessing that were required for the old 92 bis. It merely brought several documents into one, so that all parties would find it easier to follow, and that would become the statement the witness in court identified and confirmed represented their account of the truth. Now, that should not contain information which differs from the information in their 92 bis statements; it's merely getting rid of repetition and bringing into one document the contents of two or three other documents. That's one matter. The second matter is when a witness after a lapse of weeks, months, or even years comes here and is asked to look again at a statement they have made, in this case usually a 92 bis statement, and there will be times when a witness says, Oh, there's something here that isn't quite what I meant or there's something that should be added here. Now, that's new and additional material. It will occur whether we were using 92 bis statements in the original form or a consolidated 92 ter statement, because it's something that just isn't in the earlier statement of the witness or which changes something that's in there. Now, that's a process not affected by this consolidation order; it's a process which does require, as you say, quick notice to the other side of the change so that they can be aware of it before the witness commences their evidence. One of the practical problems that I think most Trial Chambers encounter with this is that so often the witness arrives very, very shortly before giving evidence, that changes are identified at the last moment, and virtually as the witness arrives in court notice is given to the Defence. That is not desirable. There may be an occasion when it's unavoidable, but if the witness were able to see the statement even a day earlier, it would obviate that last-minute notification. So we leave that in your hands to try and achieve timely notice to the Defence of any change in the statement the witness wishes to make or any additional information the witness wants to include in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That's clear, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is there anything either Defence counsel would wish to add about that? I see an indication of nothing new. Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution has created two visual aids, and the Prosecution has provided them to counsel for the accused for their review. And I'd like to take a few minutes and show them to the Trial Chamber, and perhaps hear the views of counsel on them. The first visual aid I will describe as the Ljuboten panorama and with the assistance of our case manager, we will try to show you this aid on our -- on the computer system that's in front of you. The purpose of creating this visual aid was to try to assist not just the Prosecution but the Chamber and the Defence as well as witnesses in being able to see and understand the geographical area in and around the village of Ljuboten, and in particular, particular spots where events were alleged to have occurred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So far we don't appear to have anything on our screen, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It takes a minute to come up with this particular software programme, Your Honour. Can you see a map now on your screen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. How about now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, we're getting them up now. Are Defence counsel receiving them? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: This panoramic begins with, obviously, the map of Macedonia. You can see Skopje there at the -- towards the top. Can we go to the next slide, please. There is the Skopje area with Ljuboten to the north. Can we go to the next slide, please. And now we have the start of what is actually the panoramic material itself. My case manager is now moving across what is a paragraph, a 180-degree photograph, of the Ljuboten village area. If you could move to the other side, please. And this is a view from the north of the village looking towards the south - I always get this confused - south-east, I believe. And what is interesting about this visual aid is that it is possible if you click on a particular point on the picture to go to a site in or near Ljuboten for which witnesses in this trial are going to talk about.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you click there, here we have a view close to the Ametovski -- what is known as the Ametovski house, which is one of the areas that you will hear about in this trial, and so you can get a three-dimensional view -- a 360-degree view of what people who were present at the time were able to see or not see.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you see up in the top-hand, there is something referred to Buzalak CP, that refers to a check-point that witnesses will testify about. So if we click on that, please, and then you have an image, and again a three-dimensional image of this particular spot where a number of witnesses will testify about and speak to. If we go back to the panorama, please. Go back to the right, please. And there is some other language that mentions panorama from helicopter. If you click on that, please. We have some additional views that were actually taken -- these are aerial photographs taken from a helicopter. What you're seeing now is a view of the village of Ljuboten from the south-east looking to the north, and again, different witnesses will be able to describe where they were, what they could see, where other individuals or other organisations were located at certain times relevant to the indictment. So this, just to give you very quickly, is a visual aid which we created in the hopes that it would help all parties get some perspective on the geography of the Ljuboten area and the places that are mentioned in the second amended indictment and will be discussed by witnesses. And it is our proposal to provide it to the Chamber and for use by Prosecution, Defence counsel, and by the Chamber as an aid to clarify matters during the course of the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there any concern about that proposal from either Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, not really a concern. If the Trial Chamber thinks that this material is of assistance to the Chamber, we'll obviously not object to it. Perhaps one issue of clarification, we would simply like to know when the pictures were taken which form part of this panorama.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Apostolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We do not object that proposal by the Prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the issue of when these views were taken, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: They were taken actually on two separate occasions, Your Honour. The photographer made a trip to the Ljuboten area in 2004, and then a second trip to the Ljuboten and Skopje area in the autumn of 2005.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So they're some -- each of them some years after the actual event?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber would indicate that it will certainly be prepared to receive this in the course of the trial, Mr. Saxon. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The Prosecution has prepared an additional visual aid which, for lack of a better name, we have simply called a court binder. As the Chamber is aware, in other cases the Prosecution has presented a binder or a group of materials often containing, for example, maps that are relevant to a particular case. In this case, the Prosecution felt that it would actually be more helpful and efficient to provide a series of photographs to the Chamber to keep with them and to refer to, to mark-up as you see fit, and to the Defence. We've brought some extra copies today. If I could ask the assistance of the usher to take three of them and to provide them to members of the Chamber. The Defence has been provided already with copies of them, I believe, last week. And again, if you open up the proposed court binder, you see it begins with a map of the Balkan region highlighting Macedonia; a second map simply with Macedonia; and then the first photograph --

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, Your Honour. Could the Prosecution give us a copy of the binder if they have one at this stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Please take my copy. What you will see, Your Honour, is the Prosecution has produced a copy in hard copy of the panoramic views of -- from the north of Ljuboten, from the west of -- from the south-east of Ljuboten. And then as you move through the binder, the binder contains photographs of particular spots that are mentioned in the second amended indictment and will be described, I'm sure, both by Prosecution witnesses and by Defence witnesses, particular places where the Prosecution alleges persons were either killed or mistreated, certain places where Prosecution alleges persons were detained, et cetera. And again, this was simply produced to give all parties an additional visual aid to refer to as witnesses are providing their evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is there any objection of either Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think if those pictures are part of the proposed exhibit, the Defence doesn't really see the need for such a binder. The Prosecution can seek to tender them individually or in batches as they please during the trial. But I think there's a number of issues which are going to arise in relation to some of those pictures, issues of relevance, issues of timing of the picture and that sort of thing. I don't think this material should be distributed or given to the Chamber at this stage, in our submission, in any case. If the Prosecution believes those documents to be material to their case, they should be tendered properly at trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: May I respond briefly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Apostolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would not like to repeat from what I said. I support the presentation of my colleague Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, just a clarification. The Prosecution is not seeking to tender this court binder as a Prosecution exhibit. We're simply providing it to the parties as a visual aid. Mr. Mettraux is correct, some of the photographs on this -- within the binder are on the Prosecution's exhibit list, and the Prosecution will seek to formally tender them into evidence; however, it seems to me we're talking about two different concepts here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The question of the admission of any one or more of the maps or photographs within this binder will be dealt with in the course of the trial. It does appear that it may be an aid to understanding the evidence of individual witnesses; for that purpose, it will be used initially, and gradually in time the exhibits will take over from the binder and it will come to be discarded by the Chamber by the end of the evidence, and we will be left only with the exhibits. So I think used in that sense it may prove to be of some assistance in following the evidence of particular witnesses. Thank you. Is there any further matter, Mr. Saxon?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, we have only seven minutes to go before we must break to allow the tapes to be rewound. In that time, Ms. Residovic, is there one or more matters that you would like to deal with, or Mr. Mettraux, whichever you prefer?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, perhaps I will be able to finish at least the issues which I would like to make submission about in the next seven minutes. There are essentially two issues which I would like to bring to Your Honours' attention. My lead counsel Ms. Residovic will bring a set of others to you. The first one relates to an item which we called outstanding Defence requests. We've made a number of requests to the Prosecution in writing, some of which have been responded to and those matters are, therefore, not an issue anymore. However, there are a number of others which remain pending, and there is one which we would like to bring to Your Honours' attention because it may have some consequences on the proceedings. We have made a request for information and for assistance to the Prosecution in relation to one of their proposed witnesses. This witness due to come within the next two weeks or at least among the first 15 witnesses. We have raised some serious concern about the credibility of this witness and have, therefore, sought the assistance of the Prosecution in relation to this matter. At this stage, unfortunately, we haven't received assistance from the Prosecution, at least not to the extent that the Defence sought. We have written once again to the Prosecution yesterday in relation to this matter and hope that the Prosecution will respond positively this time to this request. If the Prosecution does not assist the Defence in this matter, the Defence may have to seek a remedy from the Trial Chamber directly. We hope that will not be the case, but we want to bring it to your attention insofar as it may delay or possibly could delay the evidence of that witness. We wish not to, but we can't exclude it at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, there appears to be nothing you feel the Chamber should do or could do at the moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Not at all, Your Honour, it was simply to bring it to your attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: There is a second matter, and that will be the last for me, Your Honour, which is again simply a matter which the Defence would like to put on the record and does not seek any remedy at this stage from the Trial Chamber. It has been said in a number of cases before this Tribunal that it's for each party to decide what witness to call and what evidence to tender at trial, and we do not seek to challenge that principle. However, the Defence is very concerned in this case about what we perceive as being a very one-sided approach to the evidence that is going to be proposed by the Prosecution. Again, it is for the Prosecution to decide what evidence to call. However, the Defence will proceed on the understanding that where the Prosecution has failed to call witnesses or to tender evidence which is evidently relevant to an issue relevant to the case, it will not be permitted to seek a negative inference on the part of the Chamber where it could have called that evidence and has declined to do so. Once again, we insist that obviously the Prosecution calls the evidence which they intend to call, but we are quite concerned that evidence which clearly is relevant to this case has not been called, and we will proceed on the basis of our understanding of this principle as regard inferences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. The Prosecution is on notice about that, but as you have indicated, each party is in a position to call witnesses which they think are relevant to the case. Prosecution's obligation is wider and more extensive. It has an obligation to call all witnesses whose evidence is relevant and, to put it shortly, whose evidence the Prosecution considers to be credible and worthy of belief. And if it fails to meet that obligation, well, then that certainly can have significant consequences if there is an absence of a witness who proves to be material who was in that category. But beyond that, the -- you're speaking very hypothetically at the moment, and we really can't say or do anything until there is a practical issue to be resolved, and that's not likely to happen until after the evidence is -- of all parties is concluded and we're looking at the final addresses on the balance of the evidence. Two and a half minutes, anything further short or would you like us to adjourn now?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, at this moment I could only raise one issue; namely, the issue of translations of Defence exhibits. We have already pointed this problem out on numerous occasions as significant. Part of Defence exhibits have been translated, and we are expecting a number to be translated yet. This problem will, we expect, continue into the trial because on one hand we are continuing our investigations that are producing new exhibits; and on the other hand, which is very important, our searches of EDS, especially for documents that fall under Rule 68, have not yet been enabled. And once these searches become possible, we will be in a position to ask for more translations. For those reasons, Your Honour, we should like to ask for the leave of the Trial Chamber in exceptional situations, when we do not have an official translation of documents during cross-examination, to use a working draft translation prepared by the Defence itself for purposes of cross-examination pending an official translation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What is the delay that you anticipate for the provision of the outstanding translations? Or if you request a document, the delay you anticipate before that request is met? Can you help us there?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We cannot give you that information at this stage, Your Honour. We could ask for that information from the CLSS, and then we will be able to pass it on to you. But by judging by their practice so far, I believe that we can expect the latest documents we submitted for translation only in two or three weeks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The translation service has been working incredibly hard to meet the demand there is on -- for documents in this case because there are a number of languages that are being required, and also with other ongoing cases where there is a heavy translation requirement. So if they are managing to achieve results in two or three weeks, we are very grateful for that. That brings us back to your earlier point: You have not been able to search. Is that to do with the fact that earlier you sought documents in CD form and now are wanting them on the electronic disclosure suite?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. As you know from our earlier submissions, we received the first nine batches, both on CD and in EDS. Due to problems we encountered in Macedonia with access to EDS and certain problems encountered in Sarajevo, we asked the Prosecution to continue disclosing evidence, both in EDS and on CDs. The Prosecution continued to disclose on CDs; however, we know that searches of exhibits that are sometimes thousands of pages long do not allow for searches on a number of criteria. For that reason, we asked the Prosecution to disclose all those same documents again on EDS, so that, in view of the fact the trial is scheduled to start in April this year, we should be able to complete the entire search of exhibits disclosed to the Defence under Rule 68 in a professional manner. The Prosecution informed us that they would do so by the 3rd of April. And let me note that we never asked for disclosure in EDS to stop; we simply accepted CDs because at the beginning we had certain problems in accessing the EDS. When those problems have been removed, we asked the Prosecution to make the whole material available in EDS, which is their obligation anyway. And as I said at the last Status Conference, the Prosecution promised us that they would submit the greatest part of that material in EDS by 3rd of April. On the 4th of April, we received an e-mail from the Prosecution informing us that there are technical difficulties in transferring the whole material into EDS, and that this process will take a while. As things stand now, we still do not have -- we still do not have certain batches in EDS such as 12 to 22 and 34 to 44, and we don't see from the letter we received from the Prosecution whether the documents that were earlier contained in those batches are still there. The Prosecution also said that documents from batch 11 would not be put into EDS. On this issue, we had an exchange of letters with Prosecution, because it's very important for us to have 68 material in EDS because that is the only way in which the Defence can search by all criteria that matter to the Defence. I'm sorry. I made a mistake. We have batches 12 to 22 in EDS now, and we have 34 to 44 in EDS, according to what the Prosecution informed us. And as of today, we have over 60 batches disclosed -- sorry, as of yesterday, 72 batches.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, do I understand from what you're saying that because of your own technical problems in Macedonia, the Prosecution provided material to you in a different format, in CD form; and now that you have overcome those problems, the advantages of the EDS system are something that you need for your searching, and you only in the last few days obtained EDS disclosure of quite a number of batches of disclosure material. So you've yet to search that and you've yet then to request translations of some of that material for the purposes of your preparation. Is that the position?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, normally in the course of our entire preparations, we searched documents that have been given us on CD. But what we are trying to say is that, first of all, the Prosecution had the obligation to put all that material in EDS, regardless of the fact that they had provided it on a CD. We never asked them to stop placing material in EDS. So our position is as follows: We have already searched most of the material that is on CD and that is searchable on CD, but we know that we have not yet searched a great number of documents because searches for those documents are very difficult or impossible in CD form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, we are out of time on the tape. We must adjourn now to enable the tape to be rewound. When we return, we'll ask first, Mr. Apostolski, whether you have problems and what they may be about this, and then we'll hear from Mr. Saxon. So we will now adjourn to resume at ten minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Apostolski, is there anything you wish to -- I'm sorry, I thought you had finished on this point.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just two minutes with your leave, Your Honour. First of all, I would like to inform the Chamber that the team -- our team was joined by Mr. Dragan Godzo, legal consultant. And second, Your Honour, on the issue -- on the question you asked me, I want to be absolutely clear. On the 17th of January, 2006, our Defence team addressed a letter to the Prosecution concerning the problems that we have discussed and asked for the entire material to be made available to us also in CD form because prior to that the Prosecution was providing material, both on CD and in EDS. Since the Prosecution took their own decision, as they informed us on the 20th December, to stop providing material on CDs, we just asked them to continue that practice. We never ever asked them to stop placing material in EDS, and anyway we couldn't have done that because Rule 92 makes it incumbent upon the Prosecution to provide material in searchable form --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Did you ever ask the Prosecution to also provide the material in EDS form?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We asked the Prosecutor to provide, in addition to material in EDS, to provide material in CD form --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: When in the course of your -- in the course of your receiving CD form disclosure, did you ever then say, We are not getting EDS, we want EDS as well?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When we commenced intensive preparations for the trial in December, we noted that the Prosecution had stopped placing material in EDS, and at that point we immediately asked them to provide material in EDS as well, because just for an example the preparation for the witness who's coming next week, using CDs would mean that we have to open 74 CDs to find the name of that witness and review thousands of documents. Normally, using EDS, we would be able to do that searching just the name of that witness, and that is indispensable for preparing our defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Apostolski, anything to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to dwell on the issue of translation requested from the CLSS. I wish to inform the Court that we had in a timely fashion submitted materials of around 500 pages to the CLSS, and although they make their best of efforts, we were informed by them that until the 12th of April they will finalise the translations. Since we believe that the materials are needed, especially during the cross-examination of witnesses, I wish to inform the Court that only 50 pages of the materials were translated by the CLSS. I hope that the CLSS, although working very hard, that I will have the documents translated and that I will have them available during the cross-examination. That is what I have to say with regards to the translation of documents. With regards to disclosure of evidence by the Prosecution, the Prosecution has started making available EDS of the batches 1 to 9, and then they stopped updating and disclosing the evidence. I think -- and I would like to ask the Prosecutor to continue the practice since it is simpler and easier for us to prepare the defence. So in this respect, I would like to ask the Prosecutor once again to continue the practice of making the documents available via EDS. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: With respect to the translations, have you asked when you may receive them?

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, we have asked, and the CLSS has informed us that we would receive them translated not later than 12th of April. That was at the moment of our submission of documents for translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So you haven't inquired in the last day or two when it will be completed?

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We haven't received any answer on that by the CLSS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very briefly, Your Honour. Your Honour, it was never the Prosecution's understanding when it began to provide disclosure on individual CD-ROMs in the autumn of 2005, that the Defence counsel also expected the Prosecution to continue providing the same material, the same time on the EDS system. The Prosecution, I believe, after batch -- disclosure batch 9, stopped disclosing on both -- in both formats simply because our trial support personnel could not keep up with the workload, and because the Defence counsel had said they had preferred disclosure on CD-ROM, that was the format that we continued to use. Ms. Residovic, a moment ago, told you that in December of this [sic] year, the Defence noticed that the Prosecution had not been continuing its disclosure also on the EDS system and immediately informed the Prosecution about this. It may be that my record-keeping is faulty, but according to my records the Defence counsel for the accused Boskoski informed the Prosecution of this issue on the 12th of March, 2007. That is the letter that we have. I believe the Trial Chamber already has a copy of this letter in front of you, as well as copies of the Prosecution's response of the 15th of March. The Prosecution, since the 15th of March, has endeavoured to go back and again put all of this material also on the EDS. Simply because of technical matters, it takes time. We had hoped that a large amount of this material would have been on the EDS by the 3rd of April. There were some delays. I understand that, as of yesterday, a number of additional batches are now available on the EDS, and our technical people are continuing to work on that. At the same time, recently to avoid any -- any untimely disclosure of material, the Prosecution has been disclosing material in both formats to make sure that the Defence receives all disclosure material in a timely fashion. And as the Prosecution has said previously, we have done our very best to try to meet our disclosure obligations and to address the needs of the Defence and to facilitate their work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Saxon. This issue commenced with the proposition by leading counsel for Mr. Boskoski to inquire whether the Chamber would be prepared to allow as a matter of general practice the use of unauthorised translations for cross-examination because of difficulty in securing immediate translations of documents now taken from the EDS system, and the background to that being that the majority, the vast majority, of the disclosed information appears to have been disclosed in CD-ROM form, and that was done initially at the request of the Defence because of their technical limitations in dealing with the electronic disclosure suite form. There seem to be some 72 batches of disclosed material. Mr. Saxon says that it was after batch 8, that the Prosecution stopped EDS disclosure and moved solely to CD-ROM disclosure. There is some difference whether they were asked in December of last year or March of this year now to provide in EDS; that having occurred when the Defence teams were in the position to have proper access with their equipment to EDS disclosure. Whatever the wrongs or rights of that, it is clear that the Prosecution altered its procedure to meet the needs of the Defence, and that the -- without objection they disclosed only in CD-ROM form until, whether it be December or March is not greatly material, the request was revised, and the Prosecution has since been trying to bring its disclosure into EDS form to enable the Defence to have the advantage of the EDS form with its search facilities. The result, however it arose - and it's clearly not a matter that has arisen by failure by anybody or default by anybody - the result is that there is a great deal of material which the Defence has not been able to have translated, material which they consider important to their Defence preparation or important to their cross-examination of witnesses. The Chamber has had experience of unauthorised translations being used for cross-examination. While this may be a way of dealing with an unexpected situation, the experience of the Chamber is to indicate that this only leads to difficulty. It is surprising how often there is disagreement over the form of an unauthorised translation. At times a witness can be unfairly challenged because of the form in which an unauthorised translation exists, and the whole point of the challenge disappears as resolved when the authorised translation is received and it is seen that, in fact, the witness was not mistaken or confused but was entirely correct. And yet, the whole point of a cross-examination has gone along a false line because of a -- an often hurried informal translation, and not only is that being unfair to the witness but it also means that the point of the cross-examination is lost. So the Chamber is certainly not of the mind to agree to the idea of a practice of informal translations. We think that the interests of the -- a fair and proper trial are not going to be served by such a procedure. There will be a time occasionally when some unexpected event may require that we follow such a procedure. We don't want to rule that out as a possibility. But I can suggest to counsel from our experience that we will then lose time as we attempt to resolve what seem to be inevitable differences between the unauthorised translation and the formal considered translation. But it may be that that will be a way of overcoming some unexpected problem. But as a matter of normal practice in the trial, in our experience it will be unhelpful and could lead to a failure to do justice to one or both sides. The submissions indicate that the EDS disclosure is now virtually complete, although some still remains. That seems to mean that translations can now be sort of material documents which the Defence identifies from its searching of EDS. The experience of counsel suggests that those demands now for translation may be satisfied in two to three weeks. There's even hope that Mr. Apostolski's problems may be resolved in the near future; at least they're being dealt with. So it seems that before we get into the cross-examination of witnesses who are potentially affected by this, the efficient conduct of the trial may require that we go slow or stop for some two to three weeks. I will leave that matter at that point and deal with the other matters that need to be raised because the Chamber wants, of course, to come back to the important question of the course of evidence which is intended at the moment to commence next week. We'll come back to that later. If I could now ask Ms. Residovic whether there are other matters that she wishes to raise at this stage?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We thank the Trial Chamber, and we look forward to similar clear instructions in the future from the Trial Chamber to enable us to prepare as efficiently for the trial as possible and to avoid undue delays in leading evidence. We would also welcome clear instructions from the Trial Chamber concerning the method of introducing exhibits into evidence during trial. One of the issues we had raised with our learned friend from the Prosecution concerned our request to be informed whether the Prosecution will use any exhibits during their opening statement; and if so, which. The Prosecution gave us an affirmative answer but without any precise information. One of the issues that I would like to particularly emphasise is one that had been raised in the latest confidential motion by the Prosecution for protective measures. The Defence is fully aware of Rule 69 and the practice of this Tribunal as to how and in which way witnesses and victims are entitled to protective measures to be granted by the Trial Chamber. We will do our best to ensure that such decisions are made in accordance with the Rules and with the practice. However, the Defence has to express its disagreement with the latest remarks of the Prosecution stated in their confidential motion for protective measures. We realise it is a confidential document, and that is why the Defence will refrain from mentioning sources or the persons referred to therein. But the conclusions made in that document are of particular concern to the Defence, especially the conclusion of one of the investigators. In ongoing proceedings against a former minister of the interior of an independent and sovereign state, the Prosecution very frequently used - in support of its allegation - statements, allegations, and such that were unsupported by evidence and that were geared at creating a bad image of the accused and the government of his country, to which the Defence opposed itself providing substantiated arguments. In their latest request for protective measures, we find a statement of discriminatory nature made against one whole people, ethnic Macedonians, and this statement is made by an authorised investigator of the Prosecution, who indicates that they are capable of and prepared to intimidate witnesses who for that reason may not be willing to appear before this court. Intimidation of witnesses is a very serious allegation in our view, and if the Prosecution wants to present such information, they are required to inform the Court. But they cannot make such allegations without investigating and without informing the Court, and they cannot use such allegations in justifying their statements that some witnesses are unwilling to appear before the Court, or to testify in the way that the Prosecution would like them to, or to justify that witnesses will testify differently than previously indicated. It is the right of the Prosecution to prepare witnesses in the way they deem fit, but if their investigator claims that the witness is to be believed because one whole society, namely ethnic Macedonians, are prepared to take certain measures against a witness who would appear before this Court, then such a claim is of great concern to the Defence. It has nothing to do with professional approach to preparation of witnesses, and such claims require that investigator to appear before the Court and face cross-examination. Such claims should certainly not be placed in confidential submissions. For these reasons, our Defence believed that we had to react in a most vigorous manner. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, is there any response you wish to make?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Solely that there was certainly no discriminatory intent by any member of the Prosecution in any of its recent filings, in particular this recent motion. Second of all, of course the Prosecution is acting pursuant to the Statute and the Rules under its obligation to protect the rights and interests of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: This is a motion which has yet to be decided. I have to say that I have not yet studied the submissions on it, so I can't give any indication of my reaction to what may be there. But your observations are noted and they will be kept in mind in the next few days when that motion is concerned and dealt with. Thank you for that. Now, is there any other matter, Ms. Residovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You did ask for some discussion about exhibits. There are some exhibits which may be admitted without evidence to verify them or identify them. Obvious examples are laws of a country, statutes, regulations and the like, birth certificates, death certificates, documents of that nature. They simply be tendered from the bar table. It may be done at the beginning of a case; it may be done during an opening statement; it may be done at a convenient time during the evidence. Other documents require them to be identified and confirmed as to what they are so that the Chamber understands the nature of the document and has some basis for treating the document as authentic; and that, therefore, requires some evidence. Usually, that evidence will be provided by one of the witnesses called. When the witness has identified the document and said, Yes, I recognise that as an order issued by the chief of police, for example, the document can then be tendered as an exhibit. If there are objections, they will be dealt with at that stage.
